verses.text_old: And when We said to the angels, “Bow down for Adam,” so they bowed down, except Iblis; he refused and acted arrogantly, and he was among those who cover [the truth].
verses.text_new: And when We said to the angels, “Prostrate to Adam,” so they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused and acted arrogantly, and he was among those who cover [the truth].
verses.notes_old:
- “Bow down” for ٱسْجُدُوا: The root س ج د in the Quran consistently denotes a physical act of lowering oneself (e.g., being “with those who bow down” in 15:31). The context here (a command given to angels, followed by physical non‑compliance by Iblis) supports an act of bodily submission, so “bow down” captures that, without specifying a particular ritual form.
- “Acted arrogantly” for ٱسْتَكْبَرَ: From ك ب ر, which in Quranic usage often denotes seeking or displaying greatness over others (e.g., 7:76 “those who were arrogant said…”). Form X (استفعل) indicates adopting or exhibiting this state, hence “acted arrogantly” rather than simply “was arrogant,” to reflect the active stance of self‑magnification.
- “Those who cover [the truth]” for ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ: The root ك ف ر has the core sense of covering/concealing. Other verses (e.g., 7:76; 109:1) show it used for those who reject or deny what has come to them. Rendering it as “those who cover [the truth]” keeps the Quranic root sense of “covering” while indicating, via the bracket, that what is covered is the truth or guidance, in line with its broader Quranic usage.
verses.notes_new:
- “Prostrate” for ٱسْجُدُوا: sujūd is falling forehead-low before a greater one; pre-Islamic poetry uses it of men falling in homage before a conqueror or a king. The same command to the angels is rendered “prostrate” in 7:11, 17:61, 18:50 and 20:116, and Iblis words his refusal with the same verb (15:33: “I was not to prostrate to a mortal”). “Bow” is kept for ر ك ع (“bow down along with those who bow down”, 2:43), so the two postures stay distinct in English.

Form X (استفعل) indicates adopting or exhibiting this state, hence “acted arrogantly” rather than simply “was arrogant,” to reflect the active stance of self‑magnification.

Other verses (e.g., 7:76; 109:1) show it used for those who reject or deny what has come to them. verses.text_old: And uphold the *ṣalāh*, and give the purifying due (zakāh), and bow down along with those who bow down.
verses.text_new: And uphold the *ṣalāh*, and give the *zakāh*, and bow down along with those who bow down.
verses.notes_old:
- *ṣalāh* for ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ: kept in Arabic throughout this translation, because the Qur'an uses ص ل و for more than one English word can hold: something people establish and guard at set times (2:238, 4:103), what Allah and His angels do toward the Prophet and the believers (33:43, 33:56), and the Messenger's ṣalāt that is “a stilling reassurance” for people (9:103). The verb أَقِيمُوا (form IV of ق و م, “set upright, keep standing”) recurs with it (5:55, 27:3, 31:4, 24:56, 8:3), presenting it as something to establish and keep up, not done once; 2:45 pairs it with endurance as a source of help.
- ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ (zakāh): I translated it as “the purifying due” instead of just “alms” or “charity.” The root ز ك و in the cognate data centers on purity and moral cleanliness. In the Quranic cross‑references (27:3, 31:4, 24:56, 41:7, 5:55), zakāh is something that is يُؤْتَى / يُؤْتُونَ (“given/extended” from أتى “to come, bring, give”), and its neglect is associated with disbelief in the Hereafter (41:7). This indicates a due that purifies and is owed, not merely optional generosity. Hence “purifying due” preserves both the idea of purification and the obligatory, given‑over nature.
- وَٱرْكَعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلرَّٰكِعِينَ (and bow down along with those who bow down): This aligns with the conventional sense. The root ر ك ع in 77:48 (“when it is said to them, ‘Bow (ٱرْكَعُوا),’ they do not bow (يَرْكَعُونَ)”) clearly denotes the physical act of bowing in a devotional context. The command form ٱرْكَعُوا and the noun ٱلرَّاكِعِينَ (those who bow) naturally indicate joining a community in this act, which coheres with the surrounding call to consistent, communal devotion in 2:40–46.

verses.text_old: And when We took the firm pledge of the Children of Israel: “You shall not serve except Allah; and with the parents [show] excellence, and with the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy; and speak to people in a fine manner; and establish the *ṣalāh*, and give the purifying due.” Then you turned away, except a few of you, while you are ones who turn aside.
verses.text_new: And when We took the firm pledge of the Children of Israel: “You shall not serve except Allah; and with the parents [show] excellence, and with the near of kin, and the orphans, and the needy; and speak to people in a fine manner; and establish the *ṣalāh*, and give the *zakāh*.” Then you turned away, except a few of you, while you are ones who turn aside.
verses.notes_old:
- “firm pledge” for مِيثَاق: The root و ث ق carries the sense of binding/firmness (cognate data: “to become firm, stable, fast, strong; to tie, bind”). In 2:80 the related term عَهْد is used for “covenant,” and here مِيثَاق appears in the same thematic context, suggesting a strongly binding commitment. “Firm pledge” preserves that nuance.
- “serve” for تَعْبُدُونَ: Root ع ب د in Quranic usage (e.g., 20:14 “فَاعْبُدْنِي”) consistently covers worship as a form of devoted service and subjection. Rendering it “serve” keeps the core idea of devoted obedience to Allah, which fits the covenant context, while still including worship.
- “excellence” for إِحْسَانًا and “in a fine manner” for حُسْنًا: Both derive from ح س ن, which in Arabic and cognate evidence carries “good, excellent, strong.” Within the verse, إِحْسَانًا is directed toward parents (and, by extension, the listed groups) as a comprehensive doing of good, hence “excellence.” حُسْنًا with لِلنَّاسِ concerns speech, so “in a fine manner” captures speaking in what is good/beautiful, aligning with the same root’s sense of goodness/beauty.
- “purifying due” for ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ: Root ز ك و in the cognate set centers on purity and growth (“to be pure, clean, thrive, grow”). In 27:3 and 31:4, ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ is paired with establishing the *ṣalāh*. Rendering it “purifying due” reflects both the act of giving and its purifying function, rather than a bare “alms.”
- “ones who turn aside” for مُّعْرِضُونَ: From ع ر ض, used in 38:68 “أَنتُمْ عَنْهُ مُعْرِضُونَ” clearly meaning turning away/averting. Here it describes their ongoing state, so “ones who turn aside” preserves the active, continuous sense of deliberate aversion.

verses.text_old: Our Lord, make us two wholly devoted to You, and from our offspring [raise] a community wholly devoted to You; and show us our devotional rites, and turn back toward us. Indeed, You — You are the Oft‑returning, the Merciful.
verses.text_new: Our Lord, make us two wholly devoted to You, and from our offspring [raise] a community wholly devoted to You; and show us our *manāsik*, and turn back toward us. Indeed, You — You are the Oft‑returning, the Merciful.
verses.notes_old: - مُسْلِمَيْنِ / مُسْلِمَةً (from س ل م): I rendered these as “wholly devoted” rather than simply “submissive” or “one who submits.” Across the Quran, the root س ل م carries the sense of wholeness, safety, and being in a state of soundness or peace. In 2:131 (“Submit” / “I have submitted”), the context is Abraham’s total yielding of himself to his Lord. Here, in a prayer tied to building and purifying the House and asking for guidance in worship (2:125–127, 129), the emphasis is on complete, undivided orientation and loyalty to God. “Wholly devoted” captures both the idea of yielding and the root’s sense of completeness/wholeness, while avoiding importing later technical labels. - أُمَّةً (from ا م م): I kept “community” but with the nuance of a led, cohesive group. The cognate evidence (lead, be at the head, mother) supports the idea of a body that is gathered under a guiding principle or leadership. In this context, Abraham is asking not just for numerous descendants but for them to form a guided, coherent community oriented to God. - مَنَاسِكَنَا (from ن س ك): I translated as “our devotional rites” rather than the broader “ways of worship.” The root is associated with cultic or ritual acts of devotion. In the immediate context of the House, tawaf, bowing, and prostration (2:125), and Abraham’s building of the foundations (2:127), the request “show us our manāsik” naturally points to specific, structured acts of devotion tied to this sanctuary. - تُبْ عَلَيْنَا and ٱلتَّوَّابُ (from ت و ب): I rendered تُبْ عَلَيْنَا as “turn back toward us” and ٱلتَّوَّابُ as “the Oft-returning.” The core sense of the root in Semitic is “to turn back/return.” In the Quranic relational context between God and humans, when attributed to God it consistently conveys His repeatedly turning back toward the servant with acceptance and mercy. Keeping the “return” imagery (“turn back toward us,” “Oft-returning”) preserves the reciprocal dynamic implied in the root, rather than immediately flattening it to “accept repentance,” though that acceptance is clearly what the “turning back” entails in context. - ٱلرَّحِيمُ (from ر ح م): I translated as “the Merciful,” which aligns with the repeated formula in the cross‑references (e.g., 26:68, 26:104, etc.), where رَبَّكَ … ٱلرَّحِيمُ consistently presents God as characterized by ongoing, tender mercy. verses.text_old: We have certainly seen the shifting of your face in the sky, so We will surely turn you to a direction (of facing) that you are satisfied with. So turn your face toward the side of the Inviolable Mosque, and wherever you are, then turn your faces toward its side. And indeed those who were given the Book surely know that it is the truth from their Lord, and Allah is not unmindful of what they do.
verses.text_new: We have certainly seen the shifting of your face in the sky, so We will surely turn you to a direction (of facing) that you are satisfied with. So turn your face toward the side of the inviolable place of prostration, and wherever you are, then turn your faces toward its side. And indeed those who were given the Book surely know that it is the truth from their Lord, and Allah is not unmindful of what they do.
verses.notes_old:
- “the shifting of your face” (تَقَلُّبَ وَجْهِكَ): The root ق ل ب carries the idea of turning/alternation (cf. 26:219 “your movement among those who prostrate”). Here it indicates repeated or ongoing turning/looking, hence “shifting,” not a single turn.
- “in the sky” (فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ): The preposition فِي is kept as “in”; the context is the Prophet looking upward, and سَمَاء elsewhere is “sky/heaven.” “In the sky” preserves the spatial sense without forcing an interpretive “toward.”
- “a direction (of facing)” for قِبْلَةً: From root ق ب ل “to face, be before” (cf. 28:52 “from before it”), the noun denotes a facing-direction, not inherently “prayer” itself. I rendered it as “a direction (of facing)” to keep the core sense and avoid importing “prayer” into the word.
- “the side of the Inviolable Mosque” / “its side” for شَطْرَ: شَطْر in 2:144 and 2:149 is best taken as “side, part, sector” (a directional side) rather than simply “toward.” This fits the locative/adverbial usage and the idea of orienting oneself to a particular side of a known place.
- “Inviolable Mosque” for ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ: حَرَام from ح ر م carries the sense of forbidden/sacrosanct/inviolable. To reflect that internal semantic field, I rendered it “Inviolable Mosque” rather than leaving حَرَام untranslated.
- “unmindful” for بِغَافِلٍ: In 2:144 and its close parallel 2:149, غافل negated with ب conveys not being heedless/neglectful. “Unmindful” captures this better than simply “unaware,” since Allah’s knowledge (ع ل م) is already a given; the emphasis is on not overlooking what they do.

verses.text_old: Indeed, the Safa and the Marwah are among the marked rites of Allah. So whoever *ḥajja* the House or visits it (in devotion) – then there is no burden upon him that he go repeatedly around/ between them. And whoever volunteers any good – then indeed, Allah is Appreciative, Knowing.
verses.text_new: Indeed, the Safa and the Marwah are among the *shaʿāʾir* of Allah. So whoever *ḥajja* the House or *iʿtamara* – then there is no burden upon him that he go repeatedly around/ between them. And whoever volunteers any good – then indeed, Allah is Appreciative, Knowing.
verses.notes_old:
- شَعَائِرِ ٱللَّهِ: I rendered this as “the marked rites of Allah.” From the root ش ع ر, whose basic field (hair, fine strands) suggests something thin/noticeable, and in 22:32 شَعَائِرِ ٱللَّهِ clearly refers to visible, honored ritual markers associated with Allah. “Marked rites” captures both the ritual and the sign/marker aspect.
- *ḥajja* for حَجَّ ٱلْبَيْتَ: kept in Arabic. The root ح ج ج is heading purposefully toward something. In the Qur'an ḥajj is the journey to the House, proclaimed to people who come “on foot and on every lean camel” (22:27), and the form ḥājja is two people heading at each other in argument (2:258, 6:80). The sister languages keep a sacred journey or feast (Hebrew ḥag). “Pilgrimage” would bring in the later fixed rite, which the verse does not spell out. ٱلْبَيْت here is “the House” as a known sacred dwelling.
- ٱعْتَمَرَ: Rendered “visits it (in devotion).” Root ع م ر is “to dwell, inhabit, frequent.” Form VIII suggests undertaking a devoted visit that “populates” or frequents the House. I avoided the technical term “’umrah” and instead expressed the underlying sense of a devotional visit.
- فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِ: Rendered “there is no burden upon him.” جُنَاح, from a root of bending/inclining, in Quranic usage (e.g., 80:7 “وَمَا عَلَيْكَ”) consistently conveys “no blame / no liability.” “Burden” captures that sense of moral liability.
- أَن يَطَّوَّفَ بِهِمَا: I translated “that he go repeatedly around/ between them.” Root ط و ف is movement in circuits/going around; form V (يَطَّوَّفَ) intensifies or makes it reflexive, suggesting engaging oneself in repeated going-around. The preposition بِ with the dual pronoun “them two” (Safa and Marwah) supports the idea of ritual movement involving both, i.e., between/around them. I kept “around/ between” to reflect the circular/route nuance of ط و ف without importing external ritual detail.
- وَمَن تَطَوَّعَ خَيْرًا: Rendered “whoever volunteers any good.” تَطَوَّعَ (form V of ط و ع, to be willing/comply) indicates doing something willingly, not under obligation. Hence “volunteers.” خَيْرًا is “good” in the broad moral sense, consistent with its general Quranic usage.
- شَاكِرٌ: Rendered “Appreciative.” From ش ك ر, which in human usage is “to be grateful,” but when predicated of Allah (cf. 39:66 “وَكُن مِّنَ ٱلشَّاكِرِينَ”) implies rewarding and acknowledging good. “Appreciative” reflects that Allah recognizes and responds to volunteered good, without restricting it to human-style “thanking.”

The root ش ع ر is perceiving something fine enough to strike a hair, and a camel was marked as consecrated by a cut on its hump so the blood showed. Here the shaʿāʾir are two places, the Safa and the Marwah; in 22:36 they are the camels. “Rites” would turn them into acts to be performed.

- *iʿtamara* for ٱعْتَمَرَ: kept in Arabic, as its noun *ʿumrah* is in 2:196, beside *ḥajja* in the same clause. verses.notes_old:

- "has trusted in God": Root ا م ن carries the sense of security, trust, and confidence (supported by cognates). The Quranic usage of آمَنَ consistently combines belief with trust and reliance, so "trusted in" better reflects that than bare "believed in."
- "despite love of it": حُبّ is love; the construction عَلَى حُبِّهِ can mean "despite his love for it," fitting the ethical emphasis of giving while attached to wealth. This aligns with 92:18, where giving wealth is tied to inner purification, implying a struggle against attachment.
- "son of the path": ابْن السَّبِيل is literally "son of the path/road." The conventional sense is "wayfarer/traveler," but I kept the literal phrase and let context imply the needy traveler.
- "purifying-dues": زَكَوٰة from root ز ك و is tied in 2:174 to God "not purifying" (لَا يُزَكِّيهِمْ), and in cross-refs (27:3, 31:4, 41:7) to a due that is both financial and purifying. - "fully honor their covenant": Root و ف ي means to fulfill/complete; عَهْد (root ع ه د) carries covenant/obligation with an element of attentive observance (per cognates "know, observe, look after"). "Fully honor their covenant" captures both completion and faithful observance.
- "endure in hardship, and in harm, and at the time of conflict": Root ص ب ر fundamentally means to bear or withstand difficulty without giving way. The Quranic usage consistently emphasizes the ability to endure trials rather than passive waiting, as seen when the text asks what makes people endure punishment in the Fire.
- "mindful [of God]": Root و ق ي relates to guarding oneself, often in the Quran from God's displeasure or the Fire. "The righteous" is conventional, but the internal sense is of active God-conscious self-protection. I rendered it as "mindful [of God]" to reflect that guarding/mindfulness; the bracketed "of God" is supplied from the broader Quranic usage of متقين.

verses.text_old: O you who have attained faith, the abstaining (from food and drink) has been written upon you, as it was written upon those before you, so that you may protect yourselves.
verses.text_new: O you who have attained faith, the fasting has been written upon you, as it was written upon those before you, so that you may protect yourselves.
verses.notes_old:

- "has been written" / "was written" for كُتِبَ: The passive of كَتَبَ, whose core sense is “to write” (supported strongly by cognates), is used in 2:180 “كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ” in the sense of something formally recorded as a binding duty. The same construction appears here. Rendering it as “has been written” preserves the image of formal inscription that underlies the idea of prescription/obligation.
- "the abstaining (from food and drink)" for ٱلصِّيَامُ: The immediate context in 2:184–185 defines this practice in terms of specific days, exemptions for illness and travel, and a compensatory feeding of the poor, and then explicitly says “وَأَن تَصُومُوا۟ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ” and “فَلْيَصُمْهُ” (to fast it). The root sense is abstention; the surrounding verses clarify that the abstention here is from eating and drinking during a set period. Hence “the abstaining (from food and drink)” makes the contextual specification explicit.
- "protect yourselves" for تَتَّقُونَ: The root و ق ي carries the idea of guarding/protecting oneself from harm. In 2:21, with the same structure “لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ,” the call is to worship the Lord “who created you and those before you,” with the purpose that you adopt this self-protective, God-conscious stance. In 10:63, 41:18, and 27:53, those who “يَتَّقُونَ” are the ones thereby saved or protected. verses.text_old: It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fasting, the intimate approach to your women. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. Allah knew that you had been betraying yourselves, so He turned back towards you and remitted [it] from you. So now, be in direct contact with them and seek what Allah has written for you. And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [that is] from the dawn; then complete the fasting until the night. And do not be in direct contact with them while you are devotedly staying in the masjids. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus Allah makes His signs clear to the people so that they may be ever‑cautious.

Rendering it as “intimate approach” preserves the sense of approaching in a sexually explicit way without importing extra detail.
- "garment" for لِبَاسٌ: This aligns with 78:10, وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا (“We made the night as clothing”), where لِبَاس conveys covering, enveloping, and closeness. Here it similarly indicates mutual covering, protection, and nearness between spouses.
- "betraying yourselves" for تَخْتَانُونَ أَنفُسَكُمْ: Root خ و ن in form VIII (تَفْتَعِلُونَ pattern) indicates committing betrayal against one’s own selves. The context (they were doing something previously not allowed at night) supports “betraying yourselves” rather than a generic “deceive yourselves.”
- "turned back towards you" for فَتَابَ عَلَيْكُمْ: Elsewhere تَابَ إِلَى / عَلَى with Allah as subject indicates Allah’s turning back in mercy to the servants (accepting their return), not their act of repenting. Hence “turned back towards you” keeps Allah as the actor.
- "remitted [it] from you" for وَعَفَا عَنكُمْ: Root ع ف و in 2:52 (“Then We forgave you after that…”) shows the sense of erasing or overlooking a fault. “Remitted [it] from you” captures the idea of removing the burden of that prior wrongdoing.
- "be in direct contact with them" for بَٰشِرُوهُنَّ / تُبَٰشِرُوهُنَّ: Root ب ش ر relates to “flesh, body.” In form III here, with direct object “them” and in this context, it indicates bodily contact of a sexual nature. “Be in direct contact with them” preserves the bodily, skin-to-skin nuance without adding interpretive detail beyond the verse.
- "what Allah has written for you" for مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ: Root ك ت ب in 2:183 (“كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ” – “fasting has been written/decreed upon you”) shows that “write” can mean “ordain/decree.” Here “what Allah has written for you” keeps the wording broad, allowing for what He has allotted or decreed, without narrowing it to a specific conventional interpretation.
- "the white thread … the black thread, [that is] from the dawn" for ٱلْخَيْطُ ٱلْأَبْيَضُ … ٱلْخَيْطِ ٱلْأَسْوَدِ مِنَ ٱلْفَجْرِ: Root خ ي ط indicates “thread.” The verse itself glosses this imagery by adding مِنَ ٱلْفَجْرِ, tying the distinction to dawn. Keeping “thread” literal preserves the metaphor the verse uses.
- "complete the fasting until the night" for ثُمَّ أَتِمُّوا۟ ٱلصِّيَامَ إِلَى ٱلَّيْلِ: Root ت م م (to make complete) plus إِلَى ٱلَّيْلِ (“to the night”) coherently sets the fasting period from the clarified dawn to the onset of night.
- "devotedly staying" for عَٰكِفُونَ: Root ع ك ف carries the sense of remaining, staying, or devoting oneself in place. In context (فِى ٱلْمَسَٰجِدِ), it refers to a state of dedicated stay in the masjids; “devotedly staying” reflects both the physical stay and its devotional character.
- "limits" for حُدُودُ ٱللَّهِ: Root ح د د in the cognate data includes “hinder, prevent, forbid,” and in context these are boundaries not to be crossed. “Limits” captures that sense of divinely set boundaries.

verses.text_old: And complete the *ḥajj* and the visitation for Allah. Then if you are confined, then whatever has become easy of the guidance-offering; and do not smooth/shave your heads until the guidance-offering reaches its place of untying. So whoever among you is sick, or there is harm upon him from his head, then a ransom: from fasting, or charity, or a devoted offering. Then when you are secure, whoever has enjoyed the visitation up to the *ḥajj*, then whatever has become easy of the guidance-offering; and whoever does not find, then fasting three days during the *ḥajj* and seven when you have returned — that is ten, complete. That is for whoever's people are not present at the Inviolable Mosque. And be wary of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in retribution.
verses.text_new: And complete the *ḥajj* and the *ʿumrah* for Allah. Then if you are confined, then whatever has become easy of the guidance-offering; and do not smooth/shave your heads until the guidance-offering reaches its place of untying. So whoever among you is sick, or there is harm upon him from his head, then a ransom: from fasting, or charity, or a *nusuk*. Then when you are secure, whoever has enjoyed the *ʿumrah* up to the *ḥajj*, then whatever has become easy of the guidance-offering; and whoever does not find, then fasting three days during the *ḥajj* and seven when you have returned — that is ten, complete. That is for whoever's people are not present at the inviolable place of prostration. And be wary of Allah, and know that Allah is severe in retribution.
verses.notes_old:
- *ḥajj* for ٱلْحَجَّ: kept in Arabic. The root ح ج ج is heading purposefully toward something. In the Qur'an ḥajj is the journey to the House, proclaimed to people who come “on foot and on every lean camel” (22:27), and the form ḥājja is two people heading at each other in argument (2:258, 6:80). The sister languages keep a sacred journey or feast (Hebrew ḥag). “Pilgrimage” would bring in the later fixed rite, which the verse does not spell out.
- “visitation” for ٱلْعُمْرَةَ (al-ʿumrah): Root ع م ر indicates “dwell, inhabit, stay”; a focused religious “visit” to the sanctuary fits this semantic field and the contextual pairing with ḥajj.
- “confined” for أُحْصِرْتُمْ (uḥṣirtum): Root ح ص ر “to encircle, enclose, besiege” (cognates: “fence off, encompass, besiege”). Passive form IV here naturally yields “you are enclosed/held back, confined,” without specifying the cause.
- “whatever has become easy of the guidance-offering” for فَمَا ٱسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ ٱلْهَدْىِ (famā istaysara mina l-hady): 
  - Root ي س ر “to be easy, simple” → form X “to become easy/available.” 
  - Root ه د ي “to guide, lead” is used here in its established cultic sense of an animal/thing led as an offering; I render it “guidance-offering” to preserve the root’s guidance nuance while indicating an offering.
- “do not smooth/shave your heads” for وَلَا تَحْلِقُوا۟ رُءُوسَكُمْ (walā taḥliqū ruʾūsakum): Root ح ل ق linked to “throat, circle, ring, smoothness”; in ritual context it clearly refers to removing hair. I include “smooth/shave” to echo the underlying “make bare/smooth” nuance.
- “place of untying” for مَحِلَّهُۥ (maḥillahu): Root ح ل ل “to untie, loosen, unpack, alight, encamp, settle.” In context this is the point/place where the restrictions are “untied” and the offering is dealt with. “Place of untying” preserves that core sense rather than the more specific “place of slaughter.”
- “harm” for أَذًى (adhā): This aligns with common usage in the Qur’an (e.g., verbal or physical harm); here, context narrows it to a physical affliction “from his head.”
- “ransom” for فَفِدْيَةٌ (fidyah): Directly follows root ف د ي “to ransom, redeem, rescue”; conventional “compensation” is weaker than the core “ransom/redemption” sense.
- “devoted offering” for نُسُكٍ (nusuk): Root ن س ك is associated with ritual devotion; “devoted offering” keeps the idea of a specifically consecrated act/oblation, not just any “sacrifice.”
- “enjoyed the visitation” for تَمَتَّعَ بِٱلْعُمْرَةِ (tamattaʿa bi-l-ʿumrah): Root م ت ع relates to enjoyment/benefit; form V is reflexive/benefactive: “to enjoy/avail oneself.” I render “has enjoyed the visitation” to keep the benefit/enjoyment nuance.
- “when you have returned” for إِذَا رَجَعْتُمْ (idhā rajaʿtum): Root ر ج ع “to return”; context suggests return from the pilgrimage journey, not merely “turned back” in some abstract sense.
- “people” for أَهْلُ (ahl): Cognate data shows “family, clan, community, folk.” In context of “present at the Inviolable Mosque,” it is broader than nuclear family; “people” captures household/folk.

Here, in a Hajj-law context, it coherently refers to seeking additional benefit/provision from the Lord, not just generic “bounty.”
- أَفَضْتُمْ: Rendered “pour forth” rather than simply “depart,” following the core sense of the root ف ي ض (overflow, pour out). In 2:199 the same verb is used again for mass movement of people; the image of crowds “pouring forth” from ʿArafāt matches this semantic field and the ritual context.

verses.text_old: So when you have completed your devotional rites, then remember Allah with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance. And among the people is one who says, “Our Lord, grant us in this nearest life,” while he has, in the later life, no allotted share.

verses.notes_old:
- “Devotional rites” for مَّنَاسِك: The root ن س ك is associated with acts of devotion/ritual. In this immediate context (2:197–203) the discourse is about الحج and its actions (أَفَضْتُم, ٱلْمَشْعَرِ ٱلْحَرَامِ, أَيَّامٍ مَّعْدُودَاتٍ), so مَنَاسِك clearly refers to the set of ritual acts, hence “devotional rites” rather than a narrower or more generic term.
- “More intense remembrance” for أَشَدَّ ذِكْرًا: The root ش د د (to tighten, intensify) plus ذِكْر (remember/mention) in this comparative construction points to degree of strength rather than merely “more frequent.” Within the verse’s contrast (like your remembrance of your fathers / or stronger), “more intense remembrance” captures the heightened strength implied by شَدّ.
- “Nearest life” for ٱلدُّنْيَا: From the root د ن و (to be near, draw close), الدُّنْيَا in Quranic usage contrasts with ٱلْـَٔاخِرَة (the later/future life). Rendering it “nearest life” preserves the nearness/farness contrast embedded in the roots (د ن و vs أ خ ر) more literally than “this world.”
- “Later life” for ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ: Root أ خ ر carries the sense of lateness/following. In contrast to الدُّنْيَا as the nearer, this is the subsequent, later life; hence “later life” rather than simply “Hereafter,” to keep the temporal contrast explicit.

verses.text_old: Indeed, those who have trusted (in God) and have done the sound/wholesome deeds, and have upheld the *ṣalāh*, and have given the purifying due – for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
verses.text_new: Indeed, those who have trusted (in God) and have done the sound/wholesome deeds, and have upheld the *ṣalāh*, and have given the *zakāh* – for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.
verses.notes_old:
- "have trusted (in God)" for ءَامَنُوا: The root ا م ن in the cognate data centers on security, trust, being true/firm. Quranic usage (e.g., 84:20 “they do not يُؤْمِنُونَ” and 23:58 “believe in the signs of their Lord”) consistently conveys entrusting oneself to, and affirming as true, God and His signs. Rendering it as “trusted (in God)” keeps both the sense of belief and reliance/security implied by the root.
- "sound/wholesome deeds" for ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ: The root ص ل ح in the cognate evidence is “to be or do well, improve, change for the better,” not merely “righteous” in a narrow legalistic sense. Quranically, عَمِلُوا ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ (as in 41:8) contrasts with فساد (corruption) and denotes deeds that set things right, are beneficial, and in good order. “Sound/wholesome deeds” reflects that constructive, improving quality.
- "upheld the *ṣalāh*" for أَقَامُوا ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ: The verb from ق و م means to stand, establish, make firm; with صَلَوٰة (*ṣalāh*), other verses (27:3, 31:4) use يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ in the same sense. “Uphold” captures both establishing and maintaining it consistently, not just performing it once.
- "purifying due" for ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ: The root ز ك و in the cognate data is “pure, clean, grow, thrive.” In 27:3 and 31:4, يُؤْتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ appears alongside establishing *ṣalāh* and certainty in the Hereafter, indicating a purifying giving that promotes growth and moral cleanliness. “Purifying due” preserves both what is given and its purifying/growth aspect, rather than a bare “alms.”
- "reward" for أَجْرُهُمْ: Root ا ج ر is consistently “reward, recompense” in Quranic usage (cf. 41:8: لَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ – “for them is a reward uninterrupted”). The cognate set (hire, pay, recompense) supports this; no departure from conventional sense.
- "no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve" for لَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ: This formula recurs (2:274; 43:68; 46:13) with the same structure. خَوْف (fear) and حُزْن (sorrow/grief) are clear from both Quranic usage and cognates. The rendering follows the established internal pattern; no substantive departure from conventional meaning.

verses.text_old: O you who have believed, do not make lawful the marked-out observances of Allah, nor the declared month, nor the guided-offering, nor the garlanded ones, nor those heading for the Inviolable House seeking bounty from their Lord and approval. But when you have come out of restriction, then hunt. And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Inviolable Mosque, drive you that you commit aggression. And cooperate in goodness and conscientiousness, and do not cooperate in offence and overstepping. And be wary of Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in retribution.
verses.text_new: O you who have believed, do not make lawful the *shaʿāʾir* of Allah, nor the declared month, nor the guided-offering, nor the garlanded ones, nor those heading for the Inviolable House seeking bounty from their Lord and approval. But when you have come out of restriction, then hunt. And let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the inviolable place of prostration, drive you that you commit aggression. And cooperate in goodness and conscientiousness, and do not cooperate in offence and overstepping. And be wary of Allah; indeed, Allah is severe in retribution.
verses.notes_old:
- "do not make lawful" (لَا تُحِلُّوا): Root ح ل ل carries “untie, loosen, make free.” In 5:1–5 around it, أُحِلَّ / أُحِلَّتْ clearly means “made lawful.” Here, form IV “tuḥillū” with a negation naturally yields “do not declare/make lawful,” i.e., do not treat as open for ordinary use what Allah has set apart. This preserves the internal contrast with the surrounding أُحِلَّ / حُرِّمَ usages.
- "marked-out observances" (شَعَٰئِرَ ٱللَّهِ): From ش ع ر, whose core field is “hair” and, by extension, something finely marked or noticeable. Within Quranic context (especially 22:32–36, not quoted but same lemma), شعائر are visible, designated acts or symbols of worship. “Observances” captures ritual acts; “marked-out” reflects the root’s nuance of something distinctly signaled, without importing external ritual detail.
- "the declared month" (ٱلشَّهْرَ ٱلْحَرَامَ): شَهْر from the cognate set is “month” tied to “making known / new moon,” and حرام is “forbidden / inviolable.” Rendering as “declared month” keeps the sense of a publicly known, set-apart time, while “Inviolable” is reserved below for ٱلْبَيْتَ ٱلْحَرَامَ to avoid redundancy. This slightly departs from the usual “sacred month” by foregrounding the “declared/made-known” aspect of شَهْر.
- "guided-offering" (ٱلْهَدْىَ): Root ه د ي is “to guide, lead.” In the pilgrimage context of the passage (linked with garlands and the House), this noun denotes animals being led as offerings. “Guided-offering” keeps the guidance nuance and the sacrificial sense implied by context, instead of a bare “offering.”
- "the garlanded ones" (ٱلْقَلَٰٓئِدَ): From the idea of something hung around the neck (garlands/necklaces) marking animals or people as under a special status. Contextually paired with ٱلْهَدْىَ, so “the garlanded ones” (i.e., those marked by garlands) fits the Quranic picture of visibly designated animals, without specifying details from later tradition.

- نَقِيبًا: Rendered “overseers.” Root ن ق ب “to pierce, make holes, excavate.” The idea of “piercing through” aligns with someone who penetrates into affairs, inspects, or oversees. This fits the context of appointed figures responsible over the community’s covenantal conduct.
- أَقَمْتُمُ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ: Rendered “establish the *ṣalāh*.” Supported by 5:55 يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ, where “establish” (from ق و م “stand, set upright, establish”) captures more than merely performing; it implies upholding and maintaining it.
- وَءَاتَيْتُمُ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ: Rendered “give the purifying due.” Root ز ك و “to be pure, grow.” The Quranic pattern ties زكاة to purification and moral/spiritual growth, so “purifying due” reflects both giving and its purifying function.

  - حَسَنَةً is rendered “a good (share)” based on 2:201 and 16:122, where حَسَنَة in الدُّنْيَا clearly denotes some form of beneficial, favorable allotment in life, not merely abstract “goodness.” The parenthetical “(share)” reflects this concrete benefit nuance, but the core sense “good” aligns with conventional translations.
- “ٱلدُّنْيَا”:
  - Translated as “this nearer life” to reflect the dnw root “to be close, draw near,” and its contrast with ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ (the later / deferred life). This brings out the Quranic temporal contrast (near vs. later) rather than only “world vs. Hereafter.”
- “ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ”:
  - Rendered “the later (life)” drawing on the Axr root “late, delayed, following,” consistent with its temporal contrast to الدُّنْيَا in 2:201 and 16:122. This is a nuance rather than a departure from the conventional “Hereafter.”
- “إِنَّا هُدْنَآ إِلَيْكَ”:
  - هُدْنَا here is taken in the sense “we have turned back to You,” i.e., repented/returned. Contextually, in 7:155–156 Moses is pleading after a calamity, asking forgiveness and mercy; a sense of “returning/repenting” fits this plea. The verse immediately before (7:155) already contains “فَٱغْفِرْ لَنَا وَٱرْحَمْنَا,” so “we have turned back to You” coheres as a statement of repentance and renewed orientation toward God. This slightly departs from the conventional gloss “we have turned back” only in that it emphasizes the directional “back to You” inherent in إِلَيْكَ.
- “عَذَابِىٓ أُصِيبُ بِهِۦ مَنْ أَشَآءُ”:
  - أُصِيبُ (form IV of ص و ب) is rendered “I strike with it” to capture the idea of something hitting or reaching its target, consistent with the general semantic field of إصابة (to hit, befall). This is slightly more vivid than “I afflict,” but not meaningfully different in sense.
- “وَرَحْمَتِى وَسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ”:
  - وَسِعَتْ from و س ع is “has encompassed” to reflect spaciousness/expansiveness (cognate evidence: “be spacious, big”) and the Quranic usage of وسع for capacity and all-encompassing scope. “Every thing” follows the basic sense of كُلَّ شَىْءٍ, with شَىْءٍ as “thing” (supported by the cognate set showing “thing, anything, something”).
- “فَسَأَكْتُبُهَا”:
  - From كَتَبَ, rendered “So I will prescribe it” rather than simply “decree it,” because in 7:154 the same semantic field (نُسْخَتِهَا) is tied to written prescription (guidance and mercy in the tablets), and in 7:157 the Messenger is found “written” (مَكْتُوبًا) in earlier scripture.   - يَتَّقُونَ (form VIII of و ق ي) is rendered “those who are conscious (of Me)” rather than only “fear Me.” Cross-references like 10:63 and 23:87 show تَقْوَى as a standing, ongoing quality of those who believe and respond properly to God, involving protective awareness and cautiousness. “Conscious (of Me)” captures both fear and mindful guarding of oneself.

verses.text_old: So when the inviolable months have peeled away, then kill the associators wherever you encounter them, and seize them, and hem them in, and sit for them at every lookout. But if they turn back, and uphold the *ṣalāh*, and give the purifying due, then clear a path for them. Indeed, Allah is Ever-Covering [of faults], Ever-Merciful.

But if they turn back, and uphold the *ṣalāh*, and give the *zakāh*, then clear a path for them. Indeed, Allah is Ever-Covering [of faults], Ever-Merciful.
verses.notes_old:
- "Inviolable months": From ح ر م, which in the Qur’an carries the sense of something made forbidden/sacred (e.g., 5:2, 5:97). Here الأشهر الحرم are months under a prohibition of fighting; “inviolable” preserves the sense of being protected by a ban.
- "Peeled away": From ٱنسَلَخَ (form VII of س ل خ “to strip, flay, skin”). Elsewhere س ل خ is used for stripping day from night (36:37). The reflexive/passive form here naturally conveys the months “stripping themselves off / coming off,” i.e., passing away. “Peeled away” keeps the Qur’anic imagery of something being stripped off.
- "Associators": From ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ (root ش ر ك “to join, share”). Throughout the Qur’an, مُشْرِك refers to those who “associate” others with Allah (e.g., 6:106, 39:65). Rendering it “associators” keeps the verbal sense of actively joining partners to God, rather than a more abstract label.
- "Wherever you encounter them": حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ — وَجَدَ in the Qur’an consistently means “to find/encounter” (e.g., 18:65, 93:6). “Encounter” fits the combative context better than a purely cognitive “find out.”
- "Hem them in": From وَٱحْصُرُوهُمْ (ح ص ر “to encircle, enclose, besiege”). The cognate data and Qur’anic usage (e.g., 2:196 for being “restricted” from reaching the House) support a sense of surrounding and confining. “Hem them in” captures both besieging and restricting movement.
- "Sit for them at every lookout": مَرْصَد from ر ص د “to watch, lie in wait.” The noun indicates a place of watching/ambush. “Lookout” preserves the idea of a watching post without specifying tactics beyond what the verse states.
- "Turn back": From تَابُوا (ت و ب). Across the Qur’an, توبة is consistently “turning back/returning” from wrongdoing to God (e.g., 5:74). “Turn back” keeps the directional nuance rather than a purely legal “repent” but does not change the basic sense.
- "Uphold the *ṣalāh*": أَقَامُوا ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ — elsewhere يُقِيمُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ (27:3, 31:4, 24:56) clearly means more than merely performing; it is to establish/maintain properly. “Uphold” reflects this sustaining, establishing sense of ق و م.
- "Purifying due": ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ from ز ك و, whose cognate field is purity and growth. In 27:3, 31:4, and 24:56 it is paired with *ṣalāh* as a due that purifies and fosters growth. “Purifying due” preserves both the giving and its built-in notion of purification, rather than a bare technical loanword.
- "Clear a path for them": فَخَلُّوا۟ سَبِيلَهُمْ — سَبِيل is a “path/way” (cf. 15:76 “on an established road”). خَلُّوا سَبِيلَ in Qur’anic usage means to let someone go unhindered. “Clear a path for them” expresses removing obstruction to their way.
- "Ever-Covering [of faults]": غَفُور from غ ف ر “to cover.” In many verses (e.g., 2:192, 4:106, 5:74) غَفُور رَّحِيم describes Allah’s forgiving nature. Rendering it “Ever-Covering [of faults]” foregrounds the core sense of covering sin, consistent with the root, while the bracket clarifies the moral sense.
- "Ever-Merciful": رَّحِيم from ر ح م, consistently conveying deep, ongoing mercy (linked to womb-like compassion). “Ever-Merciful” reflects the enduring quality implied by the intensive pattern.

verses.text_old: It was not for the associators that they should inhabit / tend the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves with the denial. Those are the ones whose deeds have been nullified, and in the Fire they will be ones who abide.

verses.notes_old:
- “associators”: This renders المُشْرِكِينَ from root ش ر ك, whose core sense (from cognates) is “to join, share, partake.” In Quranic usage it denotes those who join others with Allah. This aligns with the conventional “polytheists,” but “associators” keeps the root nuance of joining/partnering.
- “inhabit / tend”: يَعْمُرُوا from ع م ر. Cognates show a primary sense “dwell, inhabit, reside,” and a derived sense “to build up, edify.” In 9:18–19 the same verb and its noun عِمَارَة are used for ongoing involvement with the mosque (presence, upkeep, service). “Inhabit / tend” captures both dwelling/frequenting and maintaining, rather than only “maintain” in a narrow, technical sense.
- “bearing witness against themselves with the denial”: شَاهِدِينَ عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِم بِالْكُفْرِ. Root ش ه د in 85:7 clearly means to be witnesses over what is done; 74:13 shows شُهُودًا as “present,” i.e., attending. Here, with عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِهِم, the sense is active self-implicating testimony. Root ك ف ر, from “cover,” in Quranic usage is denial/rejection of truth. “The denial” (rather than generic “disbelief”) preserves that they are testifying to a specific state of covered/denied truth.
- “have been nullified”: حَبِطَتْ from ح ب ط. 3:22 uses the same phrase حَبِطَتْ أَعْمَالُهُمْ “their deeds have become worthless” in both worlds. Cognate evidence (perish, be fruitless) supports “nullified” as “rendered void / without effect,” not merely “lessened.”
- “ones who abide”: خَالِدُونَ from خ ل د, whose cognates indicate remaining, lasting, staying. In 2:39 and 46:14 it describes enduring stay in Fire or Garden. “Abide” reflects ongoing remaining without over-specifying philosophical eternity beyond the text’s own term.

- “giving of drink to the pilgrim” for سِقَايَةَ ٱلْحَاجِّ: The root س ق ي in the cognate data consistently means “to give to drink, water, irrigate.” The noun سِقَايَة thus naturally denotes the act/office of providing drink. Contextually, paired with ٱلْحَاجّ (pilgrim, from ح ج ج “pilgrimage”), it points to supplying water to pilgrims.

Hence “inhabiting/maintaining” captures both dwelling/frequenting and upkeep.
- “inviolable mosque” for ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ: Root ح ر م has the sense “forbidden, prohibited, consecrated.” The phrase therefore carries the idea of a sanctuary made inviolable, not merely “sacred” in a vague sense. “Inviolable mosque” reflects the prohibition/protection nuance evident in the cognate set.

- “are not equal” for لَا يَسْتَوُونَ: Root س و ي in 32:18 appears in the same verbal pattern with the explicit gloss “They are not equal,” contrasting believer and defiantly disobedient. The same contrastive structure appears here, so “are not equal” is directly supported by Quranic usage.

verses.notes_old:
- مَسْجِدٌ: Rendered as “a place of sujūd” rather than simply “mosque.” From the root س ج د (to prostrate), the noun pattern maf‘il naturally denotes a place of prostration. In those contexts it clearly denotes an act of submissive falling down before/for someone. Rendering it as “fall down” preserves the physical sense implied by سجود while fitting the repeated narrative pattern.
- “He had been of the jinn”: كَانَ مِنَ ٱلْجِنِّ uses كان with مِن to describe belonging/being from a category. This aligns with other uses of كان + مِن (e.g., 2:34 “وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ” – “and he was of the deniers”), indicating a state or classification, hence “had been of the jinn.”
- “So he broke away from the command of his Lord”: فَفَسَقَ عَنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّهِ. The verb فَسَقَ is not glossed in the provided data, but the preposition عَنْ (“away from”) plus أَمْر (“command/order,” supported by the Proto-Semitic ‘say/command’ field and Quranic usage of أَمْر as divine command elsewhere) indicates a movement away from an imposed directive. Within this verse’s logic (contrast with the angels who complied), the sense is not merely “disobeyed” but “departed/broke away from” that command. The cognate field for ع د و (enemy) as “transgress, pass beyond limits” supports the nuance of crossing away from a boundary, which matches “broke away from.”
- “Protectors”: أَوْلِيَاء from و ل ي (w-l-y) regularly carries the sense of those who are close, supportive, in charge, or protective. - “Apart from Me”: مِن دُونِى. The root د و ن in 55:62 (“وَمِن دُونِهِمَا جَنَّتَانِ”) shows a spatial/relational “beneath/besides/below” sense. In theological contexts it regularly marks entities taken in place of or alongside God. Here, the contrast is exclusive—God vs. others—so “apart from Me” preserves that sense of taking them in His stead.
- “Enemy”: عَدُوٌّ from ع د و (ʿ-d-w) has a core sense of passing beyond/overstepping, which in interpersonal relations becomes “one who transgresses against you,” i.e., an enemy. 26:77 uses the same form: “فَإِنَّهُمْ عَدُوٌّ لِّىٓ إِلَّا رَبَّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ” where the meaning “enemies to me” is contextually clear. verses.text_old: Have you not seen that Allah—to Him submits in lowliness whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun, and the moon, and the stars, and the mountains, and the trees, and the moving creatures, and many of the people? Here the verb form suggests that the عَذَاب (commonly “punishment”) has become firmly due/realized for them. Given the cognate field of ع ذ ب (repair, set in order) and its frequent Quranic use for corrective or retributive suffering, “requital” captures both the punitive and justly-deserved, set-in-order aspect, while “has become established” reflects حَقَّ as “has taken firm effect / become binding.”

verses.text_old: Indeed, those who have covered [the truth] and who block from the path of God and from the Restricted Mosque, which We have made for the people—equally [for] the one devotedly staying there and the desert-dweller—and whoever intends in it a deviation, in wrongdoing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment.
verses.text_new: Indeed, those who have covered [the truth] and who block from the path of God and from the inviolable place of prostration, which We have made for the people—equally [for] the one devotedly staying there and the desert-dweller—and whoever intends in it a deviation, in wrongdoing, We will make him taste of a painful punishment.
verses.notes_old:
- كَفَرُوا: Rendered as “have covered [the truth].” The root ك ف ر consistently carries the idea of covering/concealing (cf. cognate data “to cover,” “to wipe off, deny, reject”). The Quranic usage in contrast with إيمان (belief) supports “covering the truth” as the underlying sense of “disbelieve,” so I make the covering nuance explicit.
- يَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ: Translated “block from the path of God.” In 16:88 and 47:1 the same construction صَدُّوا عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ clearly means active obstruction/aversion, not mere personal turning away. “Block” captures this.
- ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ: Rendered “the Restricted Mosque.” Root ح ر م in the cognate set centers on “forbidden / prohibited / consecrated.” In context (a sanctuary with special prohibitions and protections), “Restricted” reflects both its inviolability and the special rules attached to it.
- سَوَآءً ٱلْعَٰكِفُ فِيهِ وَٱلْبَادِ: Translated “equally [for] the one devotedly staying there and the desert-dweller.” Root س و ي supports “equal.” ٱلْعَاكِف suggests one who remains/devotes himself there (in context, a resident or one in retreat). ٱلْبَادِ from ب د و (desert) points to the Bedouin / outsider from open country. The phrase asserts equal entitlement of resident and nomad.
- بِإِلْحَادٍۭ بِظُلْمٍ: Rendered “a deviation, in wrongdoing.” إِلْحَاد from the idea of inclining/deviating (here from the sanctuary’s proper limits) and ظُلْم from the root “darken / oppress / wrong” (cognates show movement from darkness to injustice). The double ب- marks both as instrumental/qualifying: an intention of deviation that is in the category of ظلم. I keep both terms: “deviation, in wrongdoing.”
- نُّذِقْهُ مِنْ عَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ: “We will make him taste of a painful punishment.” This aligns with cross-references (37:38, 44:11, 84:24, 15:50), where ذ و ق + عَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ consistently conveys experiencing (tasting) a painful punishment. None

verses.notes_old:
- "magnifies": The verb يُعَظِّمْ (form II from ع ظ م) elsewhere (e.g., 69:33 اللَّهِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ) carries the sense of greatness. Form II is causative/intensive, so here it means to treat something as great, to exalt or magnify it, not merely “honor” in a vague sense.
- *shaʿāʾir* for شَعَٰٓئِرَ: kept in Arabic. The root ش ع ر is perceiving something fine enough to strike a hair, and a camel was marked as consecrated by a cut on its hump so the blood showed. The Qur'an gives shaʿāʾir to Ṣafā and Marwa (2:158), the garlanded animals (5:2) and the camels standing in rows (22:36): visible markers set apart for Allah. “Rites” would turn them into acts to be performed, where the Qur'an names places and animals.
- "God-consciousness": تَقْوَى (root و ق ي) in 23:87 (“أَفَلَا تَتَّقُونَ”) and 96:12 (“بِٱلتَّقْوَىٰ”) is tied to fearing, guarding oneself in relation to Allah. Rendering it as “God-consciousness” preserves the sense of an inner, cautious awareness of Allah that leads to guarded behavior, rather than a purely moral “piety.”
- "hearts": قُلُوب (root ق ل ب) is consistently used in the Quran for the inner core of a person (e.g., 30:59; 26:89). The conventional gloss “hearts” already captures this, so no departure here.
- "(a sign) from": The phrase فَإِنَّهَا مِن تَقْوَى ٱلْقُلُوبِ literally reads “then indeed it is from the God-consciousness of hearts.” Contextually, this means that magnifying these rites issues from, or is an expression of, that inner God-consciousness. The parenthetical “(a sign)” is an explanatory nuance, not a change of meaning.

verses.text_old: And for every community We have appointed a devotional rite, so that they may mention the name of Allah over what He has provided them of the cattle-beasts of the livestock. So your god is one God; therefore, yield yourselves to Him. And give good tidings to those who are humble and yielding.

This shows مَنسَك refers to a prescribed act of worship/ritual, not just a place. “Devotional rite” captures both the act and its worshipful nature.
- بَهِيمَةِ ٱلْأَنْعَٰمِ: Translated “the cattle-beasts of the livestock.” Elsewhere ٱلْأَنْعَٰم (e.g., 79:33, 80:32) clearly denotes grazing livestock. بَهِيمَة adds the sense of “beast/animal,” so the phrase points to the animal subset of that broader category. “Cattle-beasts of the livestock” preserves that layered expression.
- فَلَهُۥٓ أَسْلِمُوا۟: Rendered “therefore, yield yourselves to Him.” Root س ل م in form IV (أَسْلَمَ) carries the causative/reflexive sense of entering into a state of سلم (safety/wholeness/peace). In context—after affirming “إِلَٰهٌ وَٰحِدٌ”—the call is to consciously turn and submit oneself. “Yield yourselves” keeps the volitional, relational nuance rather than a bare “submit.”

Rendering as “humble and yielding” links them conceptually to “فَلَهُۥٓ أَسْلِمُوا۟” and reflects their inwardly subdued, receptive stance toward Allah.

verses.notes_old:

  - Root ن س ك appears in contexts of devoted religious action, especially in relation to God (e.g., 6:162: إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي – “my prayer and my nusuk,” clearly a religious/devotional act). This supports a sense of ritual or act of worship, not just “place.”
  - مَنسَك on the maf‘al pattern can denote either a locus or an instance/type of nusuk. Here it is something “they are ناسكوه,” i.e., actively engaged in, which fits better as a practice/rite than merely a location.
  - نَاسِكُوهُ is an active participial construction (they being “nāsiḳū” of it), indicating ongoing, characteristic engagement. Rendering as “they are devotedly performing [it]” captures both the action and its devotional character, rather than a bare “they perform it.”

  - Form III of ن ز ع (mutual pulling/struggling) in context of 22:68–69 (جَادَلُوكَ, يَحْكُمُ بَيْنَكُمْ فِيمَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ) shows a theme of dispute and contention. Thus “contend” (mutual, adversarial dispute) fits the internal pattern.
  - The emphatic nun and 2nd person object (“you”) are preserved in “let them not contend with you.”
- "The matter" for ٱلْأَمْرِ:
  - Elsewhere أَمْر is used for an affair/concern/command/task (e.g., 20:32: وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِى أَمْرِي – “in my task/affair”). Here, in context, it refers to the overall religious/ritual issue being disputed. “The matter” is consistent with that usage.

  - Root د ع و consistently carries “call/invite/summon” in Quranic usage, especially in da‘wah contexts (e.g., 23:73: لَتَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَىٰ صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ). The implied object (“them”) is supplied in English for clarity and coherence with 22:68 (“if they dispute with you…”).

- “regarding Allah” for فِى ٱللَّهِ: The preposition فِي commonly means “in,” but in many Quranic contexts it carries the sense of “in relation to / regarding” (e.g., فِي آيَاتِنَا, “concerning Our signs”). Here, “strive in relation to Allah” reads more naturally in English while preserving that relational sense.
- “striving” for جِهَاد: Root ج‑ه‑د in its basic sense is effort/struggle (cf. cognate evidence “strive / work”). Nothing in the verse restricts it to a specific type of struggle, so “striving” keeps the broader Quranic sense of exerting utmost effort.
- “truly due to Him” for حَقَّ جِهَادِهِ: حَقّ, from ح‑ق‑ق, is strongly associated with what is true, real, and binding (cf. 38:84 “فَالْحَقُّ وَالْحَقَّ أَقُولُ”). Thus the phrase indicates the striving that is genuinely His due, both in truth and obligation. “Truly due” captures that blend of truth and rightful claim.
- “selected you” for ٱجْتَبَىٰكُمْ: Cross‑reference 68:50, “فَٱجْتَبَٰهُ رَبُّهُ فَجَعَلَهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ” shows ٱجْتَبَى as a deliberate choosing out. “Selected” or “chosen out” fits this nuance better than a generic “chose.”
- “in the judgment‑way” for فِى ٱلدِّينِ: Root د‑ي‑ن relates to judging and being judged (cf. cognate set and 109:6 “لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ وَلِىَ دِينِ” where dīn is a whole way that entails accountability). Rendering دِين as “judgment‑way” highlights that it is not just “religion” in a vague sense, but a way of life under divine judgment.
- “constraint” for حَرَجٍ: Root ح‑ر‑ج carries the idea of tightness, narrowness, or difficulty. “Constraint” reflects this sense of being hemmed in, rather than merely “difficulty” as a generic hardship.
- “creed” for مِلَّةَ: Root م‑ل‑ل is tied to utterance/speaking (cognate evidence “speak, utter”), and مِلَّة in the Quran consistently refers to a doctrinal path or professed way (e.g., مِلَّةَ إِبْرَاهِيم). “Creed” captures a spoken, professed way of belief and practice.
- “those who submit” for ٱلْمُسْلِمِينَ: Root س‑ل‑م is about safety, wholeness, peace (cf. 37:109 “سَلَامٌ عَلَىٰٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ”). - “judgment‑way” implied again in “before and in this”: The phrase “مِن قَبْلُ وَفِى هَٰذَا” is left general in English (“before and in this”) to cover prior revelation and this current discourse, without importing external specifics.
- “witness / witnesses” for شَهِيدًا / شُهَدَاءَ: Root ش‑ه‑د is consistently about witnessing and testifying (cf. 100:7 “لَشَهِيدٌ”). “Witness” and “witnesses” preserve that legal‑testimony nuance.
- “uphold the *ṣalāh*” for فَأَقِيمُوا ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ: Root ق‑و‑م (stand, establish) plus صلوة (*ṣalāh*/worship; cf. cognates linking to *ṣalāh*) suggests not just performing but maintaining it properly. “Uphold the *ṣalāh*” reflects the establishing aspect.

verses.text_old: And those who are doers for the zakah.
verses.text_new: And those who are doers for the *zakāh*.
verses.notes_old:

The core semantic field from Quranic usage and cognates is purity/growth through giving. verses.text_old: And when it is said to them, “Fall down in humility to the All-Merciful,” they say, “And what is the All-Merciful? Shall we fall down in humility to what you command us?” And it only increased them in fleeing aversion.
verses.text_new: And when it is said to them, “Prostrate to the All-Merciful,” they say, “And what is the All-Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?” And it only increased them in fleeing aversion.
verses.notes_old:
- ٱسْجُدُوا۟ — Rendered “fall down in humility” rather than simply “prostrate.” Cross-references like 53:62 “So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]” and 84:21 “they do not prostrate” show سجود as a bodily act of lowliness before God, but the broader context here (rejection of the divine name and quality ٱلرَّحْمَٰن) suggests emphasizing the humility aspect, not just the physical motion.
- ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ — Translated “the All-Merciful.” This aligns with conventional glosses, but is reinforced here by 25:59 immediately before, where ٱلرَّحْمَٰنُ is the creator of the heavens and the earth and the one established over the Throne, and by 1:3 and 55:1 where the same form clearly denotes an intensive, all-encompassing mercy.

verses.notes_old:

The contrast is not framed in this verse as a legal definition but as two different kinds of “increase”: one that does not “grow with Allah” and one that does. Hence I kept the semantic field “increase/growth” throughout for internal consistency.
- “زَكَوٰةٍ”: The root ز ك و in cross-references (92:18; 41:7) and cognate evidence carries the sense of purity and also growth/thriving. The Quran uses زكاة as a specific type of giving, but also tied to purification (92:18 “يَتَزَكَّىٰ” – “to purify himself”). I retained the conventional term “zakah” but left it untranslated to preserve its technical nuance while recognizing its root sense of purifying/growing giving, which fits the contrast with ربا as a different kind of “increase.”

verses.notes_old:

- “bowing down”: For تَسْجُدَ (root س ج د), other verses like 53:62 (“So prostrate to Allah…”) show that سجود is a physical act of lowly submission. “Bowing down” captures the bodily act without adding explicit cultic overtones beyond the text.
- “with My two hands”: بِيَدَيَّ is a clear dual of يَد (hand). Cognate data (Akkadian idu; Aramaic יד) confirms “hand” as the basic sense, often associated with power or agency. The verse itself, however, presents it as “two hands,” so the translation keeps the dual literally as “My two hands” rather than abstracting to “power.”
- “Did you act arrogantly”: أَسْتَكْبَرْتَ is Form X from ك ب ر, which in 23:46 appears with عَالِينَ: “they were arrogant (ٱسْتَكْبَرُوا) and were a people عَالِينَ.” The derived form indicates adopting or showing greatness, hence “act arrogantly.”

term_surveys.canonical_english_new: head toward; argue (ḥajj kept in Arabic)
term_surveys.translation_note_old: Conventional translations render حَجّ as 'pilgrimage'. However, upon tracing the root ح-ج-ج across all 33 occurrences we find a consistent pattern of argumentation, disputation, and making a case through evidence or demonstration. In 6:83, for instance, the Qur'an speaks of "Our argument which We gave to Abraham" using this same root in an explicitly disputational context, while in 40:47 the damned "argue with each other" in Hell. We translate as 'argue', which encompasses pilgrimage as one form of arguing — a physical demonstration and embodied case for one's devotion — while honoring the Qur'an's consistent usage across contexts of debate, proof-making, and evidential presentation.
term_surveys.translation_note_new: Conventional translations render حَجّ as 'pilgrimage'. The root ح-ج-ج is heading purposefully toward something. As ḥajj it is the journey to the House, proclaimed to people who come on foot and on every lean mount (22:27), with the new crescents as its fixed times (2:189) and in well-known months (2:197). As ḥājja and ḥujja it is two parties heading at each other in argument, and the proof that lands: a man disputes Abraham about his Lord (2:258), and Allah gave Abraham His ḥujja against his people (6:83).
